results.resolution: Whole row re-pointed to the Ptarmigan Traverse approach from the Cascade Pass trailhead: approach (supersedes r12), approach_logistics, road, itinerary (3 sourced days, no numbers), overview, beta, hazards, gear, glacier fields, watch_out, data_quality gaps, requiredSkills, bivy; timing/dist_km/gain_ft/loss_ft nulled; pin 0 moved to the trailhead, pins 1-2 removed, Kool-Aid Lake and Yang Yang Lakes added, Agnes Creek line cleared.
results.summary: Rimrock Ridge now goes in the way the record says: up the Ptarmigan Traverse from Cascade Pass to the Le Conte-Sentinel col, not up Agnes Creek.
results.evidence: Seventh pass, 2026-10-01. r12 had a two-source approach op (1982 Mountaineer annual + Beckey: reached from the Ptarmigan Traverse near Sentinel / the Le Conte-Sentinel saddle, then east along the crest) held because the pins, line, trailhead and day 1 still described Agnes Creek. This pass found the replacement content. (1) Re-read the 1982 annual PDF in full (pp.92-93): the party reached the traverse after a first ascent near Bench Lake, climbed German Helmet on Aug 24, then 'Traversing north of Sentinel then east' climbed Primrose and Rimrock Peak (7,240 ft, 'narrow north arete, class 4') on Aug 25. It names no trailhead. (2) Trailhead: the Ptarmigan Traverse's north start is the Cascade Pass trailhead at the end of the Cascade River Road (NPS trail page: the trail is 'a popular starting point for ... the Ptarmigan Traverse'; SummitPost; rocknropenw; Alpine Ascents; marcmicatka). Road: NPS 23.1 mi from SR 20 at Marblemount, paved first third, narrow steep last 3 mi; WTA 23 mi 'to the end', go straight where 20 turns; SummitPost the same (22 mi, 3,660 ft). Coordinate: WTA 48.4754,-121.0751; rocknropenw 48.4753,-121.0754; OSM trailhead node 48.47549,-121.07516. Elevation 3,600: AAI and rocknropenw (SummitPost 3,660). (3) Day plan from Cascade Pass, agreed by Alpine Ascents (day 1 Cascade Pass -> Cache Col -> Kool Aid Lakes; day 2 Red Ledges, Middle Cascade Glacier roped, Spider-Formidable col -> Yang Yang Lakes; day 3 onto the Le Conte Glacier with Le Conte and Sentinel), marcmicatka (same three days, roped on the glacier under Formidable, day 3 back up to the ridge and down snow below Le Conte), rocknropenw (day 1 Kool-Aid Lake ~6 h, day 2 Yang Yang Lakes; 'the Le Conte / Sentinel Col at 7300 ft, at the top of the Le Conte Glacier'), SummitPost (stages Cascade River -> Kool-Aid -> Yang Yang -> White Rock; lakes 'about a day's hike apart'), AAI (same camps in reverse; Kool-Aid 6,120, Yang Yang 5,830, Cascade Pass TH 3,600; Red Ledges class 3, exposed, easy unless snow-covered), Mountain Project (waypoints: Cache Col, Kool-Aid Lake bivouac 1, Red Ledges under Arts Knoll 'very narrow and exposed', Spider-Formidable Col, Yang Yang Lakes bivouac 2, Le Conte Glacier and Sentinel/Old Guard; crevasses and bergschrunds). No miles, gain or hours written (none stated by two sources for this direction; nothing computed). (4) Pins: Kool-Aid Lake GNIS 1521763 48.438716,-121.045848 vs OSM camp node 48.43929,-121.04623 (~70 m); Yang Yang Lakes GNIS 1528348 48.392597,-121.056932 vs OSM camp node 48.39177,-121.05693 (~90 m). Elevations: Kool-Aid 6,120 (AAI) / 6,100 (rocknropenw); Yang Yang 5,830 (AAI) / 5,840 (rocknropenw). Fivemile and Swamp Creek Camps are on Agnes Creek, >5 km from the new line (rule 1 + rule 2: removed with the approach change). Cache Col (GNIS 48.448465,-121.052904 vs OSM 48.44871,-121.05232) has coordinates but only one stated elevation (AAI 6,900), so it is not added; the Le Conte-Sentinel col has no published coordinate. (5) Consistency: the new approach is GLACIATED, so every field saying 'never touches a glacier' / 'no glacier travel' / 'no rope' would contradict it and was rewritten (glacier kit: rocknropenw gear list helmet/ice axe/crampons/harness/prusiks/rope; roped travel: Alpine Ascents, marcmicatka; crevasses: Alpine Ascents, Mountain Project). Agnes/Stehekin-only content (bushwhack and PCT-bear hazards, Hemlock bridge watch-out, Stehekin camps in bivy, timing, the 40.23 km round trip, 4,300 ft gain/loss) was dropped or nulled. The Flat Creek trail from Stehekin (the old bivy main entry, and a 1968 Sierra Club outing) is closed for hazard trees per the row's own entry, so under rule 2 it loses. (6) North arete class: still single source (1982 annual: class 4). listsofjohn (Cloudflare check, not bypassed), Internet Archive (no Stevens-Rainy volume; search-inside unavailable on the 1973 item) and Google Books API (quota exhausted) gave nothing; grade NOT changed. OWNER FOLLOW-UPS (not written, no two sources or conflicting): access.* still describes High Bridge/Stehekin permits, fees, closures (Sisi Fire / Agnes trails, 'This approach cannot be used'), land manager and passRequired; sources disagree on parking (WTA: none; rocknropenw: Northwest Forest Pass) and on camp permits beyond Cache Col (SummitPost 2011 + rocknropenw: none needed outside the park). emergency.* still names the Stehekin ranger station, boat evacuation and Lake Chelan hospital. season/best_season/seasonal_guidance/climate mention Agnes Creek/Stehekin in places; crowds/difficulty/commitment untouched. r12's approach op is SUPERSEDED by this file's (same expect) - apply r13, not r12.

ops.expect: Access to the trailhead is by boat, floatplane, or trail only — no road connects Stehekin to the outside world. Take the Lady of the Lake ferry from Chelan up 50-mile-long Lake Chelan to Stehekin Landing (Lady Express ~2.5 hrs, Lady II ~4 hrs). From there it is 11 miles up-valley on Stehekin Valley Road to High Bridge Guard Station (1,600'), the trailhead for the Agnes Creek Trail (PCT); for the 2026 season the historic High Bridge shuttle bus is not scheduled to run, so plan to walk the road, bike it, or book a private shuttle. From High Bridge, follow the Agnes Creek Trail (PCT) roughly 8-9 miles up-valley (Three-Mile Camp near mile 3, Swamp Creek Camp near mile 8.5), then leave the trail and bushwhack east into the upper Agnes Creek/Blue Basin drainage toward the base of the ridge. Off-trail brush is thick for roughly the first 1,000' of gain and eases above about 4,000'; fording Agnes Creek or Spruce Creek on downed logs is typically required to reach the basin.
ops.value: No trail reaches Rimrock Ridge. The way in is the north end of the Ptarmigan Traverse. Start at the Cascade Pass trailhead at the end of the Cascade River Road and climb the Cascade Pass trail, then follow the traverse's climbers' path over Cache Col and down to Kool-Aid Lake, the usual first camp. The next day crosses the exposed Red Ledge below Arts Knoll and the crevassed Middle Cascade Glacier (rope up) to the Spider–Formidable col, then drops to Yang Yang Lakes, the usual second camp. On the third day the traverse climbs back to the Le Conte ridge and up the Le Conte Glacier to the col between Le Conte and Sentinel at its head. The parties on record left the traverse here, passed north of Sentinel Peak and followed the ridge east along its crest; the ridge is the divide between Flat Creek and the West Fork of Agnes Creek. Beyond the traverse the line is cross-country alpine ground with no path, and no detailed description of it is published. The Agnes Creek trail (PCT) from High Bridge runs up a different valley and does not lead to the ridge.

ops.expect: Rimrock Ridge is a minor, infrequently climbed 7,255' crest in the Ptarmigan Mountains subgroup of the Glacier Peak Wilderness, rising above the headwaters of Agnes Creek in Chelan County. It sits near Agnes Mountain (8,115') and Devore Peak, on the dry east side of the Cascade crest above Lake Chelan and the Stehekin valley (USGS Agnes Mountain 7.5' quad). The ridge has essentially no recorded ascents or published trip reports online; most parties visiting this upper-Agnes-Creek basin are headed for the better-documented Agnes Mountain or Gunsight Peak via the same approach.
ops.value: Rimrock Ridge is a remote, rarely climbed crest in the Glacier Peak Wilderness, mostly above 6,500 ft, forming the divide between Flat Creek and the West Fork of Agnes Creek and running east and north-east from Old Guard Peak. Its high point lies a little over 3 miles north-east of Sentinel Peak. No trail reaches it: the few parties on record came onto its west end from the Ptarmigan Traverse near Sentinel Peak.

ops.note: Divide + runs from Old Guard: both. >6,500 ft and 3.2 mi NE of Sentinel: Beckey; GNIS Rimrock Ridge points sit east of Sentinel. Approach: both.

ops.expect: No published or online route beta exists specifically for Rimrock Ridge. It lies about 2.3 miles from Old Guard Peak in the same remote LeConte Glacier / Ptarmigan Traverse massif, so an ascent would likely involve terrain similar to nearby Old Guard and Sentinel Peaks: long, unmaintained approaches from Stehekin (via Agnes Creek or Flat Creek) or a cross-country detour off the Ptarmigan Traverse, followed by off-trail alpine scrambling to the summit.
ops.value: No detailed route description exists for Rimrock Ridge. The recorded parties reached its west end from the Ptarmigan Traverse near Sentinel Peak and followed the crest east over its summits on cross-country alpine ground.

expect.name: Park Creek Camp, at the valley road
expect.notes: This is the camp the park itself points overnight parties to now that Flat Creek is shut, and that closure is the single most important planning fact for this peak. The camp at the Flat Creek trailhead, which would otherwise be the obvious base, has its access trail closed for hazard trees and has dropped out of both the park's camp list and its booking system; no reopening date has been given anywhere. Park Creek sits lower down the same road, so using it lengthens an approach that is already long — you are walking further to the trailhead each morning rather than sleeping at it. Note this is the camp on the valley road where the Park Creek trail leaves it, not the stock camp several miles up that trail toward the pass. The four-person cap is worth checking against your party before you plan around it.
expect.water: Park Creek at the camp, reliable all season.
expect.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit, arranged by email before you travel as above. A total campfire ban has been in force across the entire Stehekin valley since the end of June, covering anything that produces ash including propane fire pits, with no end date announced — so the ring here is out of use regardless of what the camp table says about fires. Gas and propane stoves are still allowed, with clearance around them and a working shut-off valve. Confirm the ban's status when you get the permit.
expect.capacity: Two sites, each capped at four people, so this is a small-party camp only. No stock. It has a fire ring, which is not the same as permission to use it right now.

expect.name: Bivouacs in the upper Flat Creek basin, beyond the end of the trail
expect.notes: Rimrock Ridge is an obscure summit and should be described as one. It forms the southern rim of the upper Flat Creek valley — everything falling off its far side goes into the West Fork of Agnes Creek instead — and it looks across at the glaciated back of the crest that the classic traverse walks along. Accounts of that traverse do not mention it, because climbers up there are facing the other way, and no ascent account of it was found at all. The approach is the whole difficulty: boat, shuttle, most of a day walking the old road, a gentle valley trail of about four miles that gains only a few hundred feet through old growth and through forest still recovering from a fire early this century, and then trailless ground up the headwaters to whatever line goes. The trail ends well short of the head of the valley and the summit is beyond where it ends. Budget four days minimum for something that would be an afternoon if a road came near it, and build the itinerary around the boat timetable rather than the climbing, because a missed sailing costs a day at each end. Late summer into early autumn is the window; the valley walk is snow-free long before the head of it is.
expect.water: Creek and snowmelt throughout the basin, which is at least the easy part — this is a wet valley fed off the glaciers on the crest above it, and running water is not the problem here that it is on a ridge camp.
expect.permit: The agency changes on this trail, and it is the thing most likely to be got wrong. The Flat Creek trail leaves the national park about two miles up and passes into the Glacier Peak Wilderness under the national forest, so the ground you actually camp and climb on is Forest Service. Checked against the boundary rather than assumed: the summit itself lies inside that wilderness. It takes a free self-issue permit filled in at the trailhead rather than a park permit, with no reservation and no fee, and a party limit of twelve counting people and pack animals together — larger than the park's limit down in the valley, and a rare case where walking further gets you a looser rule. Groups over twelve must split and stay a mile apart. Your park permit still covers the valley camps you slept in getting there, so a full trip needs both. There is no park cross-country zone for Flat Creek; that is not a gap in the record, the zone system simply does not reach here because the ground is not the park's. Standard wilderness practice otherwise: durable surfaces, well back from the water, pack out what will not bury, and no fires.
expect.capacity: No established camping and no site count. There is nothing up here. The trail stops, and a party going on picks whatever flat gravel, slab or old moraine it can find in the head of the valley. Anyone describing a camp here is describing a place they happened to sleep.

expect.name: Tumwater Camp, Stehekin valley road
expect.notes: The first camp of consequence above the shuttle's turnaround at High Bridge, and its job on this trip is to absorb the arrival day. The boat gets in around the middle of the day and the last shuttle up the valley goes in the late afternoon, so nobody sensibly starts a twenty-mile approach on day one — you ride to High Bridge, walk a short way up the old road, and sleep in flat riverside forest with no view and no alpine character at all. It has a history of high-water damage and was closed after a bad flood, though it stands in the park's current camp table; confirm it is genuinely open when you arrange the permit rather than assuming, because there are not many camps up here and losing one reshapes the whole itinerary.
expect.water: The Stehekin River is right there and runs all season. Treat it — it is a big glacial river carrying silt and everything else off the drainage.
expect.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, covering Lake Chelan National Recreation Area as well as the park. There is no permit desk in Stehekin — the visitor centre at the landing does not issue them and is closed. For a trip starting in the valley the permit is arranged by email with the park's wilderness office, sent early on the morning before your start date, with a short mandatory video to watch and a signed copy to print and carry. There is no cell service in Stehekin, so all of that has to happen before you get on the boat. Food lockers are provided at these valley camps and no bear canister is required.
expect.capacity: Two sites, each taking up to six people, so six is the party ceiling. No stock. Assigned by night on the permit.

expect.name: Shady Camp, Stehekin valley road
expect.notes: Further up the old road than Tumwater and the only camp on this stretch that is held back from the booking system entirely, which is exactly why it is worth knowing about. A party whose permit request comes back with a hole in the middle of the itinerary can often fill it here. It is another flat forested river camp with nothing to look at, used purely for position. Note that the road above the washout is closed to bicycles as well as vehicles — the upper section is decommissioned or maintained as a non-motorized, non-mechanized trail, so the obvious idea of riding the old roadbed to save a day is not permitted. It is walking or stock, and that is what makes this approach as long as it is.
expect.water: River water beside the camp, dependable through the season and needing treatment.
expect.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, arranged the same way as the rest of the valley — by email to the wilderness office the morning before you start, since nothing can be issued in Stehekin itself. Because the site is walk-up rather than reservable, it cannot be locked in months ahead; ask for it in that same email.
expect.capacity: A single site taking up to eight people. No stock. Walk-up only — this one takes no reservations at all, which makes it the useful fallback when everything else on the road is booked out.
